ENT CLINICAL NOTE

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  • 3-hour history of chest tightness and mild shortness of breath following an upper-respiratory viral illness; no new food, drug, or environmental trigger identified.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  • Cold last week → residual cough, sore throat, runny nose improving.  
  • Tight chest and wheeze began ~3 hours ago and persist.  
  • No chest pain; symptoms worse with exertion (stairs); none at rest.
- ENT symptoms:
  • Sore throat last week; improving.  
  • Runny nose last week; improving.  
  • Patient said “Yeah” when asked about sore ears (unclear – possible mild ear symptoms; not elaborated).  
  • Denies dysphagia, odynophagia, drooling, throat-closing sensation, voice change, facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling, stridor, or noisy breathing.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  • Asthma since childhood; severe exacerbation at age 16–17 requiring intubation and several-day hospital stay.  
  • No recent ED attendances.  
  • No prior adrenaline injections.
- Allergies and current medications:
  • Allergies: dust; hay fever; childhood milk-protein allergy (resolved). No drug allergies.  
  • Current/rescue medications:  
    – Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler – ran out 1 week ago; dose/route/frequency not documented.  
    – Clenil Modulite steroid inhaler – ran out 1 week ago; dose/route/frequency not documented.  
    – Spacer device “somewhere at home”; not in use.  
  • No oral medications currently.
- Social context:
  • Student; recently returned from university.  
  • Consult conducted in private setting; no accompanying person.

Objective:
- Observable swelling: None reported or visualized.
- Airway/breathing: Patient reports wheeze and chest tightness; no stridor, no respiratory distress at rest.
- Mental status: Alert, conversational.
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- Physical examination findings: None documented.
- Presence of another person: None.

Assessment:
- Likely asthma exacerbation triggered by recent viral upper-respiratory infection and 1-week non-adherence due to running out of both preventer (Clenil) and reliever (Salbutamol) inhalers.  
- No features of anaphylaxis or upper-airway obstruction.  
- ENT involvement minimal; sore throat/runny nose attributed to resolving URI.  
- Risk factors: prior severe asthma requiring intubation; current lack of inhalers.

Plan:
- Prescriptions issued:  
  • Salbutamol inhaler (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
  • Clenil Modulite inhaler (dose/route/frequency not documented).  
  • 5-day course of oral steroids: “two tablets in the morning” (exact drug/strength not documented).  
  • Spacer device with usage instructions.
- Advice given:  
  • Resume regular preventer (Clenil) once symptoms settle; use Salbutamol PRN.  
  • If Salbutamol required more often than every 3 hours, or if worsening shortness of breath, chest tightness, dizziness, or other concerning symptoms develop, seek immediate medical attention (doctor or emergency services).  
  • Rest from work/studies; self-certify first 7 days; further sick note offered if needed.  
  • Read steroid information leaflet and monitor for mood change, rash, nausea, headache, or hyperglycemia.
- Follow-up:  
  • Obtain prescribed medications “within the hour.”  
  • No specific ENT or allergy referral arranged; follow routine asthma review once recovered.
- Emergency contact instructions: “Any deterioration in your symptoms, like worsening shortness of breath… seek further medical attention anytime.”

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing/expected elements:
  – No vitals (HR, RR, BP, SpO₂, peak flow).  
  – No objective chest or airway examination.  
  – Exact names/doses of prescribed oral steroids not documented.  
  – Detailed allergy list (foods, drugs, latex, etc.) incomplete.  
  – No current asthma action plan or auto-injector (not indicated but often assessed).  
  – Vaccination status (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19) not discussed.
● Internal conflicts: None identified; unclear single “Yeah” response to “sore ears.”  
● Transcript quality: Clear overall; brief audio dropouts (“cutting in and out”) noted but did not affect key clinical content.
